scenes.text: Eleven fifty eight in the morning. Moscow, Idaho. A nine one one dispatcher picks up a call from a rented house on King Road.

marks.label: A 911 call is placed from 1122 King Road

scenes.text: A young woman was crying. Something has happened in our house, she said, and we don't know what.
Another voice took the phone. One of the roommates is passed out, she said. She's not waking up.
And then, almost as an afterthought, one line that changed everything that followed. They saw some man in their house last night.
By the time that call was placed, four University of Idaho students had been dead for roughly eight hours.

marks.label: A housemate wakes to sounds upstairs

scenes.text: Their names were Kaylee Goncalves, Madison Mogen, Xana Kernodle and Ethan Chapin. This film is about the record their case produced, and what that record still doesn't say.

scenes.chapter:
Chapter one
What the record is
scenes.text: Almost everything the public knows about this case came from documents. Not from a trial, because there never was one.
A probable cause affidavit. A plea agreement. A judgment. And, four years later, a hand-written petition from a maximum security prison.
Those four documents are the entire spine of this episode. Where they are silent, we will say so, and we will stop there.
The first document, the affidavit, describes a night in a rented house three blocks from campus.
Investigators placed the killings between about four and four twenty five in the morning. Nobody called for help at four.

timeline.title: From the affidavit and released messages

marks.label: A housemate wakes to sounds upstairs
Calls and texts to the victims go unanswered
They call someone outside the house

scenes.cap: Every one of these times is in the record.

scenes.text: One housemate told investigators she woke to sounds from a room upstairs. She opened her door more than once. On one of those occasions, she described standing in frozen shock as a masked figure in black walked past her toward a door.
She was twenty years old. She had been asleep. Every account of what she did next has to start with those two facts.
For nearly eight hours, the house was quiet, and the people still alive inside it believed the people who weren't were sleeping.

kinetic.sub: between the first sounds and the first call

scenes.chapter:
Chapter three
One piece of leather
scenes.text: The case turned on a single object, left behind in the room where two of the victims were found.
A tan leather knife sheath. A Ka-Bar sheath, lying beside Madison Mogen.
The knife itself has never been recovered. The sheath was what mattered, because of a detail almost too small to picture. The snap.
The Idaho State Lab found a single source of male DNA on the button snap of that sheath. One person. Not a mixture.

kinetic.sub: male DNA on the sheath's button snap

scenes.text: And here is the problem investigators had in November of twenty twenty two. They had a profile. They had no name to attach it to.

scenes.chapter:
Chapter four
How they found him
scenes.text: What happened next is the part of this case that will outlive it, because it is now used across the country.
No criminal database contained that profile. So the FBI went somewhere else. Public genealogy databases, where ordinary people upload their own DNA to find relatives.

tree.title: Investigative genetic genealogy
rows: Unknown male DNA on the sheath snap

scenes.text: The technique does not look for the suspect. It looks for his cousins, and then it builds family trees outward from them, until the branches close in on one household.

tree.title: Investigative genetic genealogy
rows: Unknown male DNA on the sheath snap

scenes.text: That household was in Monroe County, Pennsylvania. In late December, investigators collected trash from outside the home of a family named Kohberger.
Comparing what they found there to the profile from the sheath, the lab concluded that a male in that household could not be excluded as the biological father of the person who left DNA on that snap.

Prosecutors later put a number in the record. At least five point three seven octillion times more likely to be his than an unrelated person's. That is the figure in the filing. It is not our claim, and it is not a statement about guilt on its own.

scenes.chapter:
Chapter five
The car and the phone
scenes.text: DNA identified a person. Two other kinds of record put him in motion.
The first was a white Hyundai Elantra, a twenty fifteen model. Investigators traced its movements on the morning of the thirteenth.
scenes.cap: Out, and back, inside three hours.

scenes.text: Five days after the killings, that car was re-registered in Washington state, and given a new licence plate. Before that, it carried Pennsylvania plates.

marks.label: Observed moving toward Moscow and back

scenes.text: The second record was a phone. According to the affidavit, his phone had connected to towers in the area of that house at least twelve times before that night, beginning the previous August.

kinetic.sub: cell-site records cited in the affidavit, from August 2022

scenes.text: He was a doctoral student in criminal justice at Washington State University, ten miles away, across the state line. He was arrested in Pennsylvania on December thirtieth, six weeks after the killings.

scenes.chapter:
Chapter six
The line that wasn't in it
scenes.text: Now the part of the record that lawyers, not viewers, tend to notice.
The affidavit that justified his arrest described the DNA comparison. It did not mention that genetic genealogy had been used to find him in the first place.
scenes.source: Probable cause affidavit — omission later acknowledged
scenes.cap: The technique that found him is not in the document that arrested him.

scenes.text: The lead detective later acknowledged that omission. Prosecutors confirmed the technique in filings months afterward, in June of twenty twenty three.
The defence spent much of the next two years attacking exactly that. What the databases were, whose rules applied, and what a judge should be told about how a suspect was found.

timeline.title: The fight over how he was found

marks.label: Affidavit unsealed — no mention of genealogy

scenes.text: That argument was never resolved by a jury, because the case never reached one.
On July second, twenty twenty five, two and a half years after the killings, he pleaded guilty.
Four counts of first degree murder, and one count of burglary. In exchange, the state took the death penalty off the table.

kinetic.sub: Plea agreement, State of Idaho — July 2, 2025

scenes.text: Three weeks later, on July twenty third, he was sentenced to four consecutive life terms without the possibility of parole, plus ten years for the burglary.
scenes.cap: Four consecutive life terms. No parole.

scenes.text: He was given the opportunity to speak at that hearing. He declined.

Which means the families left that courtroom with a sentence, a signed agreement, and no stated reason. There is no motive in this record. Anyone who tells you otherwise is filling a silence with a guess.
For a year, that was the end of it. Then, on July twenty seventh, twenty twenty six, a new filing arrived.
A petition for post conviction relief, filed from the Idaho Maximum Security Institution. Hand-written. And filed by him, representing himself.

kinetic.sub: Petition for post-conviction relief — filed July 27, 2026

scenes.text: In it he asks for a new trial. He alleges that his lawyers failed him, and that his guilty plea was not knowing or voluntary, because it was induced, he writes, by unkept promises.

kinetic.sub: Petition for post-conviction relief — his allegation

scenes.text: Specifically, he claims he was promised things about prison life that did not follow. Contact visits. Movement. Work. And that he was told what he calls elaborate lies about life on death row.
scenes.cap: These are his allegations. They are unproven.

kinetic.sub: Petition — unproven allegations by the petitioner

scenes.text: Every one of those claims is his. None of them has been tested, and the person making them has an obvious interest in the outcome. That is not a dismissal. It is the standard the record itself applies.

Legal commentators have generally described his chances as poor, and pointed to the appeal waivers inside the agreement he signed. That is commentary, not a ruling. The petition is live as this is published.
One of the mothers said publicly that her family is ready for a trial. After four years of documents, that sentence carries a weight nothing in the filings does.

So this is what the record holds. A sheath with one man's DNA on the snap. A car photographed going out and coming back. A phone that had been there before. A signature on an agreement. And a hand-written page asking to take it back.
And one thing it does not hold, anywhere, in four years and thousands of pages. A reason.

kinetic.sub: no motive was ever established publicly

scenes.text: Four students went to sleep in a rented house on a Saturday night. The document that explains why has never been filed.

This is Criminal Record, where every case is built from the primary record and nothing else. If this one held your attention, the next file we open is the one where the paperwork itself was the crime. Subscribe, and you'll see it first.
